expertise: Algorithms and Data Structures, Efficient Graph Algorithms, Practical Hash Functions
talktitle: Compact oracles for reachability and approximate distances in planar digraphs
abstract: It is shown that a planar digraph can be preprocessed in near-linear time, producing a near-linear space oracle that can answer reachability queries in constant time. The oracle can be distributed as an O(log n) space label for each vertex and then we can determine if one vertex can reach another considering their two labels only.The approach generalizes to give a near-linear space approximate distances oracle for a weighted planar digraph. With weights drawn from {0, …, N}, it approximates distances within a factor (1 + ε) in O(log log (nN) + 1/ε) time. Our scheme can be extended to find and route along correspondingly short dipaths.

Speaker: Jarosław (Jarek) Byrka
title: Professor
honor:
STOC 2010 Best Paper Award,
Witold Lipski prize
expertise: Discrete Optimization, Location and Covering Problems, Network Design, LP-Rounding Approximation Algorithms, Randomized Rounding Techniques
abstract:
We propose a single rounding algorithm for the fractional solutions of the standard LP relaxation for k-clustering. As a starting point, we obtain an iterative rounding (3p+1)/2-Lagrangian Multiplier-Preserving (LMP) approximation for the k-clustering problem with the cost function being the p-th power of the distance. Such an algorithm outputs a random solution that opens k facilities in expectation, whose cost in expectation is at most (3p+1)/2 times the optimum cost. Thus, we recover the 2-LMP approximation for k-median by Jain et al. [JACM'03], which played a central role in deriving the current best 2 approximation for k-median.

Then, we show how to convert the LMP-approximation algorithms to a true-approximation, with only a (1+ε) factor loss in the approximation ratio. We obtain a (3p+1)/2+ε-approximation algorithm for k-clustering with cost function being the p-th power of the distance, for p≥1. Further we also show how to obtain improved approximation in the Euclidean metric setting, where we get 1.71955-approximation for k-median and 11/3+ε-approximation for k-means.

Speaker: Ho-Lin Chen
title: Professor
expertise: Algorithm Design, Molecular Computing, Algorithmic Game Theory
talktitle: Self-Stabilizing Leader Election in Population Protocols
abstract:
Population protocols provide a simple model of distributed computation in which anonymous agents with limited memory interact in pairs to perform collective tasks. Leader election is one of the fundamental problems in this model. In the self-stabilizing variant, the protocol must converge to a configuration with a unique leader from any initial configuration and maintain this property thereafter. Despite its simple formulation, self-stabilizing leader election presents significant challenges, particularly when the agents have limited memory or the network size is unknown.

In this talk, I will present a series of results on self-stabilizing leader election in population protocols. We first show that a constant number of states suffices to solve the problem on rings of arbitrary sizes, and extend this approach to tori and regular graphs. Although these protocols require exponential convergence time, they demonstrate that self-stabilization is possible with extremely limited memory. We then turn to complete graphs and investigate the tradeoff between stabilization time and the number of states. In particular, we obtain an asymptotically optimal linear-time protocol with a linear number of states, as well as faster protocols that achieve sublinear and even logarithmic stabilization time at the cost of substantially larger state spaces.

Finally, I will discuss several recent developments that further improve these tradeoffs, including near-time-optimal protocols with polylogarithmic and polyloglog states on rings, and new approaches that significantly reduce the state complexity of sublinear-time protocols on complete graphs.

Speaker: Koustav Bhanja
title: Postdoc Researcher
talktitle: Beyond Gomory–Hu: Maximum Information about All-Pairs Minimum Cuts in $O(n)$ Space
abstract:
For an undirected weighted graph $G=(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices, an $(x,y)$-mincut $C\subset V$ is the least value cut satisfying $C\cap \{x,y\}=\{x\}$. The classical Gomory–Hu tree is one of the most elegant structures in graph algorithms. It encodes an $(x,y)$-mincut for every pair of vertices $x,y$, using only $O(n)$ space. However, it stores only one ‘arbitrary’ mincut per vertex pair, even though there can be exponentially many. This raises a fundamental question: How much information about the families of all-pairs mincuts can be encoded while retaining Gomory–Hu compactness? 

In this talk, I will discuss two recent results of ours that settle this question in a strong sense:
All-pairs Nearest Mincuts. The nearest $(s,t)$-mincut is the unique inclusion-wise minimal one among all $(s,t)$-mincuts containing $s$. We introduce the nearest mincut hierarchy, an $O(n)$-space structure that encodes the nearest mincut for every pair of vertices. Moreover, given any $(u,v)$ pair, it reports the nearest $(u,v)$-mincut in $O(n)$ time.

All-pairs X All-pairs Mincuts. We further extend the nearest mincut hierarchy to encode the maximum possible information about the entire family of $(x,y)$-mincuts, simultaneously for all vertex pairs $x,y$, while retaining $O(n)$ space.

We present an $O(n)$ space structure that, given any four vertices $x,y,u,v$, reports an $(x,y)$-mincut separating $u$ and $v$, whenever one exists, in $O(n)$ time. Thus, information about $\Theta(n^4)$ choices is represented using just $O(n)$ space. Also, requiring the mincut to place $u$ on the side of $x$ and $v$ on the side of $y$ needs $\Omega(n^2)$ space, even for a fixed pair $x,y$.

The technical part of this talk will focus on the first result on all-pairs nearest mincuts. I will discuss the main technical ideas behind the nearest mincut hierarchy. The emphasis will be on how it encodes all-pairs nearest mincuts in $O(n)$ space rather than how to recover them efficiently. In particular, I will illustrate how the classical connectivity carcass of Dinitz and Vainshtein [STOC ‘94], originally designed for Steiner mincuts, can be interestingly used here beyond the Steiner mincuts scope.

I will also discuss the immediate applications of both results to all-pairs mincuts sensitivity oracles. They together yield $O(n)$ space oracles that determine how the mincuts between vertex pairs change upon the insertion or failure of any edge. The first result handles only edge insertions, while the second can handle edge failures also. Together, they resolve an open question of Baswana and Pandey (SODA ‘22): whether all-pairs mincuts sensitivity oracles exist that occupy subquadratic space and achieve $o(m)$ query time simultaneously.

Coauthors: The first result is joint work with Yotam Kenneth-Mordoch and Asaf Petruschka, appearing in SODA ’27. The second result is joint work with Merav Parter and Asaf Petruschka, submitted to STOC ’27.

Speaker: Ben Tsun-Ming Cheung
title: Assistant Professor
talktitle: Space-efficient Streaming Algorithms for Two-Dimensional Congruence Testing
abstract:
Geometric congruence asks whether two point multisets are identical up to translation and rotation. This problem is a fundamental building block for many computer vision applications, and its time complexity has been extensively studied in the RAM model.

To investigate the space efficiency aspect of this problem, we study geometric congruence in the streaming model with finite-precision rational inputs. In contrast to the conventional algorithmic setting, the input coordinates are rational numbers of bounded bit length presented in a stream with limited access, and the goal is to solve the problem using as little memory as possible.

We discuss several space-efficient randomized algorithms for 2D congruence testing, including a one-pass sublinear-space algorithm, and some two-pass polylogarithmic-space algorithms. To achieve the space efficiency, we employ several number-theoretic approaches to compress the relevant high-precision information into moderate-precision statistics.

On the hardness side, we use communication complexity methods to establish a matching space lower bound. Moreover, for another natural variant, approximate congruence testing, we show that no low-pass streaming algorithm can solve the problem without using linear space. This establishes a gap between exact and approximate congruence testing in the streaming model and illustrates that the exact-input constraint is a necessary restriction.

Speaker: Chao-Kai Chiang
title: Assistant Professor
expertise: Learning Methods for Imperfect Supervision, Noisy Labels, Online Learning, and Bandit Feedbacks
talktitle: Weakly Supervised Learning: A Contamination Perspective
abstract:
Among the flourishing research of weakly supervised learning (WSL), we recognize the lack of a unified interpretation of the mechanism behind the weakly supervised scenarios, let alone a systematic treatment of the risk rewrite problem, a crucial step in the empirical risk minimization approach. In this talk, we introduce a framework providing a comprehensive understanding and a unified methodology for WSL. The formulation component of the framework, leveraging a contamination perspective, provides a unified interpretation of how weak supervision is formed and subsumes fifteen existing WSL settings. The induced reduction graphs offer comprehensive connections over WSLs. The analysis component of the framework, viewed as a decontamination process, provides a systematic method of conducting risk rewrite. In addition to the conventional inverse matrix approach, we devise a novel strategy called marginal chain aiming to decontaminate distributions. We justify the feasibility of the proposed framework by recovering existing rewrites reported in the literature. https://openreview.net/forum?id=RGsdAwWuu6

About the Speaker:
Dr. Chao-Kai Chiang is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU), where he leads the Resilient Intelligence Lab (RIL). His research interests include weakly supervised learning, learning with label noise, learning under distribution shift, and multi-armed bandits. His research aims to develop practical and theoretically grounded machine learning methods for reliable learning from imperfect data in changing environments.

Speaker: B.H.A.F. Bob Krekelberg
title: PhD Candidate
talktitle: On the FirstFit Algorithm for Online Unit-Interval Coloring
abstract:
Graph coloring is a classical problem in combinatorial optimization, with a rich history of both algorithmic and structural results. In the online setting, vertices arrive one by one and must be assigned colors irrevocably, without knowledge of future arrivals. One of the most natural algorithms for this problem is FirstFit, which assigns each arriving vertex the smallest available color. Despite its simplicity, understanding the precise performance of FirstFit remains challenging, even on highly structured graph classes such as interval graphs.

In this talk, I will discuss recent progress towards understanding the performance of FirstFit on unit interval graphs, where intervals have equal length and may be open or closed. I will introduce a new counting technique that generalizes the classical neighborhood bound. The key idea is to identify critical intervals that lead to sharper bounds on the number of colors used by FirstFit. Using this technique, we show that FirstFit uses at most 2ω colors when all endpoints are integral, and at most ⌈(7/3)ω⌉ − 2 in the general case, where ω denotes the optimal number of colors.

Speaker: Hsiang-Hsuan Liu [Dec 7]
title: Assistant Professor
expertise: Combinatorial Optimization, Online Algorithms, Approximation Algorithms
talktitle: Scheduling Unwanted Tasks with Locality by Routing
abstract:
Academics have their own research interests and teaching preferences. Unfortunately, not all teaching tasks are equally desirable. When assigning teaching tasks to colleagues, the workload depends not only on who teaches a course but also on what other courses they teach.

Motivated by such scheduling problems, we study a strongly NP-hard routing problem on trees. Multiple servers serve requests located at vertices, starting from a common source and ending at their respective terminals. Each server travels free of cost along its source-to-terminal path and pays for traversing other edges. The objective is to minimize the maximum cost among the servers. Balancing their loads is challenging because the cost of traversing an edge may vary across servers.

We propose a polynomial-time 4-approximation algorithm using a two-phase parametric pruning framework. The first phase partitions requests into packets, while the second assigns these packets to servers. The main challenge is to relate the quality of the partition and the resulting load balance to the hypothetical optimal values in the framework. For general graphs, we establish that achieving an approximation ratio better than 2 is impossible unless P = NP.

The problem generalizes unrelated machine scheduling and other classical scheduling problems, providing a graph-based framework for modeling scheduling with locality.

This is joint work with Fu-Hong Liu, published at MFCS 2024.

Speaker: Hsiang-Hsuan Liu [Dec 10]
title: Assistant Professor
expertise: Combinatorial Optimization, Online Algorithms, Approximation Algorithms
talktitle: The Power of Cycles in Online Firefighting
abstract:
The firefighting game is a fundamental problem in theoretical computer science, modeling the containment of a spreading process under limited defensive resources. In each round, an algorithm may protect a set of vertices by placing firefighters on them, preventing the fire from spreading to those vertices. Vertices that are never reached by the fire are said to be saved. The goal is to maximize the number of saved vertices. While the offline version has been extensively studied, much less is known about the competitive complexity of the online variant, where the underlying graph is known in advance but the number of available firefighters in each round is revealed online.

We study how graph structure governs the power of the adversary in the online firefighting game. On trees, the problem is known to be 2-competitive (Coupechoux et al., 2019), a result that relies on a strong structural alignment between the online algorithm and the offline optimal solution throughout the process. We show that this alignment breaks down as soon as cycles are present. In particular, the algorithm and the offline optimal solution may break a cycle differently, or even break different cycles, and therefore operate on fundamentally different residual graphs. As a result, the adversary gains additional leverage by steering the process along residual graph structures that no longer admit a direct comparison between the algorithm and the offline optimal solution.

Our main result shows that the presence of a single cycle already increases the competitive complexity of the firefighting game dramatically. We first show that even on a tadpole graph (a cycle with a tail), no deterministic online algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio better than Ω(√n), where n is the number of vertices. We complement this lower bound with matching upper bounds by designing an O(√n)-competitive online algorithm for 1-almost trees, that is, graphs obtained from a tree by adding at most one edge. Furthermore, we extend our framework to cactus graphs and prove that, despite the presence of multiple cycles, the competitive complexity remains Θ(√n) as long as the cycles do not share edges. Together, these results yield a tight characterization of the adversarial power induced by cycles with non-overlapping edges. Finally, considering that cactus graphs have treewidth of 2, we study a variant in which firefighters are released in pairs, that is, an even number of firefighters becomes available in each round. Surprisingly, the competitive complexity is significantly reduced to 3-competitive for this setting.

This is joint work with Max Hugen and Bob Krekelberg, published at MFCS 2026.

Speaker: Felix Ohnesorge
title: Postdoc Researcher
talktitle: A Constructive FPT Algorithm for Integer Cone Optimization with Convex Costs
abstract:
We give a deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm for integer cone optimization with convex costs. 

Given $\tau$ rational polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^{d+k}$, we combine generators whose first $d$ coordinates are integral and whose remaining $k$ coordinates may be fractional.
Each generator has a convex cost depending only on its integer coordinates.
We minimize the total cost of nonnegative integer combinations subject to arbitrary rational linear constraints on the full typewise aggregates and generator counts.
Our algorithm runs in time
\[
    2^{\tau\log(\tau+1)\,2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)},
\]
where $|I|$ is the total binary input length. It constructs an optimal representation using at most $2^{2d+1}$ distinct generators per type.
The number $k$ of continuous coordinates contributes only to the polynomial input factor.

For a single generator type, the running time becomes $2^{2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}$.
Applications include constructive FPT algorithms for Cone and Polytope Intersection, high-multiplicity bin packing, vector bin packing, and makespan minimization on uniform and unrelated machines.
The double-exponential dependence on $d$ is tight for Point-in-Cone and both bin-packing problems assuming $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}$.
The mixed-integer formulation also yields additive EPTASs for makespan minimization, machine covering, and envy minimization on identical machines, and additive schemes fixed-parameter tractable in $1/\varepsilon+\tau$ on uniform machines.

Speaker: Peter Rossmanith
title: Professor
talktitle: When Exact Algorithms Are Elusive: What Should We Relax?
abstract:
When an exact algorithm is too expensive, the usual response is to seek a polynomial-time approximation algorithm. But a different relaxation may give a more useful guarantee. I will give several examples of how problems can be relaxed, then examine three ways to relax the problem of covering a graph with k shortest paths. 

We can keep k shortest paths and cover almost all vertices; cover every vertex while allowing up to 2k shortest paths; or keep k paths and full coverage while allowing each subpath to be at most 1 + ε times as long as a shortest path. Each version admits a fixed-parameter algorithm that succeeds whenever an exact k-path cover exists. These results show how the choice of what to relax can matter as much as the algorithm itself.

Speaker: Chen-Yu Wei
title: Assistant Professor
talktitle: Proximal Regret and Proximal Correlated Equilibria: A New Tractable Solution Concept for Online Learning and Games
abstract: Learning and computation of equilibria are central problems in game theory, theory of computation, and artificial intelligence. In this work, we introduce proximal regret, a new notion of regret based on proximal operators that lies strictly between external and swap regret. When every player employs a no-proximal-regret algorithm in a general convex game, the empirical distribution of play converges to proximal correlated equilibria (PCE), a refinement of coarse correlated equilibria. Our framework unifies several emerging notions in online learning and game theory-such as gradient equilibrium and semicoarse correlated equilibrium-and introduces new ones. Our main result shows that the classic Online Gradient Descent (GD) algorithm achieves an optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ bound on proximal regret, revealing that GD, without modification, minimizes a stronger regret notion than external regret. This provides a new explanation for the empirically superior performance of gradient descent in online learning and games. We further extend our analysis to Mirror Descent in the Bregman setting and to Optimistic Gradient Descent, which yields faster convergence in smooth convex games.

Speaker: Marcus Wilhelm
title: Postdoc Researcher
expertise: Graph Algorithms, Parameterized Complexity, Randomized Analysis, Geometry
talktitle: Diameter Computation Between Theory and Practice
abstract:
The diameter of a graph is defined as the maximum distance between any two vertices. Despite being a fundamental graph problem with many applications, there remains a large gap between well-understood theoretical algorithms and the approaches used for diameter computation in practice.

In this talk we consider the iterative fringe upper bound (iFUB) by Crescenzi et al., and gain an intuition for its good performance on real-world networks with the exception of torus-like geometric graphs. To overcome this limitation, we develop a new algorithm with provable performance guarantees on (torus) random geometric graphs. Finally, we explore results from  engineering an efficient implementation of this algorithm and see how well it performs in practice.

Speaker: Yi-Shan Wu
title: Postdoc Researcher
expertise: Machine Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Statistical Learning Theory
talktitle: A Sample-Efficient Way to Learn with Theoretical Guarantees
abstract: How can we learn effectively from limited data while retaining meaningful performance guarantees? A standard approach optimizes a training objective over the full dataset, often using mini-batch SGD. This talk presents a sequential approach that partitions the training data into subsets and learns in stages. What is learned at each stage guides the next, while risk guarantees are carried forward along the learning path.

Speaker: Wei-Hsuan Yu
title: Associate Professor
talktitle: The maximum size of binary three-distance codes
abstract:
We prove that for every (n\ge 24), the maximum size of a binary code of length n with at most three distinct Hamming distances between distinct codewords is (\binom{n}{3}+n). This settles the three-distance case of the few-distance conjecture for the binary Hamming cube, allowing the distances to vary with n. The code consisting of all words of Hamming weight one or three attains the bound and has distance set ({2,4,6}). The threshold (n=24) is sharp, since the dual binary Golay code of length (23) has (2048>\binom{23}{3}+23) codewords and only three nonzero distances. The proof combines a cubic polynomial in the inner product with inertia and linear programming bounds. A rank argument handles the remaining exceptional case in odd dimensions.

This is joint work with Valjakas Djaljapayan and Hao Huang.

Speaker: Julian Zimmert
title: Senior Research Scientist
talktitle: Change of Measure in Online Linear Optimization
abstract:
Online Linear Optimization (OLO) is a fundamental problem solved with canonical algorithms such as Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) or Online Mirror Descent (OMD). 

Many sequential decision problems are solved by reducing them to OLO. While this strategy has proven extremely successful, regret components external to OLO sometimes lead to suboptimal overall regret. In a surprising number of distinct problems, a change-of-measure would immediately resolve the issue. 

This talk presents the linear change-of-measure technique for FTRL and OMD. Although this technique isn't new, it is surprisingly little known and people continue to derive complicated solutions to problems that change-of-measure trivially resolves.
